content.title: About
content.content: Cheese fondue is a classic Swiss dish consisting of melted cheese into which pieces of bread, vegetables or meat are dipped. The traditional blend uses Gruyère and Emmental, with white wine, garlic and spices. It is served hot in a communal pot.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Fondue originated in the Alpine regions in the 19th century as a way to use leftover cheese.
The traditional serving vessel is a wooden pot kept warm by a small candle.
Switzerland celebrates National Fondue Day on March 11.
There are many variations: meat fondue (Bourguignonne), chocolate fondue, and vegetarian versions.
The original recipe calls for dry white wine, which gives the dish its distinctive aroma.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: The cheeses used in fondue provide a high amount of calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Melted cheese supplies high‑quality protein that supports muscle maintenance.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Cheeses contain vitamin B12 and riboflavin, which help the nervous system function.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Fermented cheeses may contribute beneficial bacteria to the gut microbiome.

items.title: Phosphorus content
items.content: Phosphorus in cheese aids cellular energy metabolism.

items.title: High in fat and calories
items.content: Fondue is rich in saturated fats, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: People who cannot digest lactose may experience discomfort.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Cheeses are often salty; those with hypertension should limit intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve fondue in a warmed pot and dip bite‑size pieces of baguette, boiled potatoes, pickled vegetables or cooked meat. A splash of wine or a dab of mustard can enhance flavor. Prepare small batches to keep the cheese smooth.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool leftover fondue, transfer it to an airtight container, and refrigerate for up to 2 days. Reheat gently over low heat while stirring to prevent curdling.

content.title: About
content.content: A flavored decaffeinated iced latte is a cold coffee beverage made from roasted decaf coffee beans, milk, and natural flavorings. It retains the creamy latte profile without the stimulating effect of caffeine, making it suitable for evening consumption.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeinated coffee is produced either by extracting caffeine from regular beans or by using naturally low‑caffeine varieties.
Iced latte first gained popularity in the United States in the 1990s as a response to the growing demand for cold coffee drinks.
Natural flavorings (vanilla, caramel, nut) are often added after extraction to preserve their aromatic qualities.
Decaf drinks may contain up to 5 mg of caffeine per serving, far less than a regular latte (about 70 mg).
Cold brewing helps retain aroma because lower temperatures do not degrade volatile compounds.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Even without caffeine, decaf coffee retains polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: A cold, water‑rich beverage contributes to the body’s fluid balance.

items.title: Lower acidity
items.content: The decaffeination process often reduces acidity, making the drink gentler on the stomach.

items.title: Enriched with milk
items.content: Milk adds calcium, vitamin D, and protein, supporting bone health.

items.title: Suitable for caffeine‑sensitive individuals
items.content: Ideal for people avoiding stimulants while still enjoying coffee flavor.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Those with lactose intolerance or milk allergy should opt for plant‑based alternatives.

items.title: Added sugar in flavorings
items.content: Some flavored syrups contain added sugars; check the label if you watch sugar intake.

items.title: Residual caffeine
items.content: Although low, the small amount of caffeine may still affect highly sensitive individuals.

items.title: Caloric content
items.content: Cream or sweet syrups increase the drink’s calories.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the decaf iced latte well‑chilled over ice, optionally adding natural syrup or spices such as cinnamon or nutmeg. Plant‑based milks—almond, oat, soy—can be used as alternatives.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared beverage in the refrigerator for no more than 24 hours. If using a decaf coffee concentrate, keep it in a sealed container in a cool place and follow the manufacturer’s shelf‑life recommendations.

ham-potatoes-and-vegetables-including-ca.title: Ham, Potatoes and Vegetables (carrots, broccoli, dark‑green leafy)

content.title: About
content.content: The dish consists of boiled or baked ham, boiled or roasted potatoes and fresh vegetables – carrots, broccoli and/or dark‑green leafy greens. The combination of protein, complex carbs and fibre makes it a nutritious and balanced meal.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Ham is traditionally made from pork loin that is smoked or baked, giving it a distinctive aroma.
Potatoes are one of the world’s most consumed root vegetables; they are rich in starch and vitamin C.
Broccoli contains sulforaphane, a compound studied for its potential anti‑cancer properties.
Dark‑green leafy greens (spinach, kale) are high in vitamin K, essential for blood clotting.
This combination is often used in diets to sustain energy and aid recovery after workouts.

items.title: Rich in protein
items.content: Ham provides high‑quality animal protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes supply slowly digestible carbs that help maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: High in dietary fibre
items.content: Broccoli and leafy greens are abundant in fibre, supporting digestive health.

items.title: Vitamins and minerals
items.content: The meal offers vitamin C, vitamin K, folate, potassium and magnesium, which support immunity and heart function.

items.title: Antioxidant compounds
items.content: Sulforaphane in broccoli and carotenoids in carrots help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Ham often contains a lot of salt; people with hypertension should limit its intake.

items.title: Presence of nitrites
items.content: Smoked ham may contain nitrites; choose products without added artificial preservatives.

items.title: Pork allergy
items.content: Some individuals may have an allergy or intolerance to pork.

items.title: Potential food poisoning
items.content: Improperly stored potatoes can develop solanine, a toxin that causes gastrointestinal upset.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the dish hot as a main course or cold as a salad. Cube the ham, slice the boiled potatoes, add blanched broccoli, grated carrots and leafy greens. Optionally dress with olive oil, lemon juice, salt and pepper.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the prepared dish in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Store ham and vegetables separately to prevent excess moisture. For freezing, separate the components and store in bags for up to 2 months.

content.title: About
content.content: A muffin is a small, cake‑like baked good made from a blend of rye flour, wheat flour, eggs, milk, and a modest amount of sugar. The English version is known for its denser crumb and the distinctive rye aroma, often complemented by a slight tang from a sourdough starter.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Rye muffins appeared in England in the 19th century as a quick snack for laborers.
Traditionally they were served with butter or jam, but modern recipes frequently add dried fruit or nuts.
Rye flour gives the muffin a darker color and a characteristic earthy flavor that sets it apart from wheat‑based versions.
In some English regions the muffin is called a “sourdough bun,” highlighting the use of a fermented dough.

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: Rye flour contains more fiber than wheat, supporting healthy digestion.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: The rye component causes a slower rise in blood sugar, beneficial for glycemic control.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are essential for metabolism.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Rye contributes a modest amount of iron, supporting blood formation.

items.title: Moderate protein content
items.content: The muffin offers plant‑based protein that can help meet daily needs.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Both rye and wheat flours contain gluten, making the product unsuitable for people with celiac disease.

items.title: High calorie density
items.content: Even small servings can be calorie‑rich due to butter and sugar.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some recipes include salt, which should be considered by those limiting sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Muffins can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, sliced and spread with butter, jam, or cream cheese. They pair well with hot tea or coffee.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer keeping, refrigerate (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 2 months).

content.title: About
content.content: A wheat (or cracked wheat) and raisin muffin is a soft baked good made from whole‑grain wheat flour or cracked wheat, sweetened with natural raisins. It has a gentle aroma, a lightly sweet flavor, and a tender crumb that combines the nutrition of whole grains with the quick energy of simple sugars.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Whole‑grain wheat retains the bran and germ, making the muffin more nutrient‑dense than those made with refined flour.
Raisins provide natural sweetness and contribute small amounts of iron and potassium.
Traditional recipes bake the muffins in an oven, but they can also be prepared in a microwave or steamed.
Some versions replace refined sugar with honey or maple syrup to highlight the fruit notes of the raisins.
Wheat contains the trace mineral zinc, which supports immune function.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain wheat and raisins supply fiber that aids digestion and promotes satiety.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs from wheat provide a steady release of energy, helping to maintain stable blood‑sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat is a good source of thiamine, niacin, and folate, which are important for metabolism and nervous‑system health.

items.title: Contains minerals and antioxidants
items.content: Raisins add iron, potassium, and polyphenols that have antioxidant properties.

items.title: Heart‑friendly potential
items.content: Fiber and plant compounds in whole grains may help lower cholesterol levels.

items.title: Wheat allergy or gluten intolerance
items.content: People with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity should avoid this muffin or choose a gluten‑free version.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Raisins increase the overall sugar load, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: Muffins can be relatively high in calories due to oil and sugar, so moderation is advised.

items.title: Choking hazard for young children
items.content: Small raisin pieces may pose a choking risk for toddlers.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy the muffin as a snack on its own, split it and spread with cottage cheese, yogurt, or nut butter. It pairs well with tea or coffee. For a softer texture, warm it briefly in the microwave.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store muffins in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 3 days. For longer storage, keep them in the refrigerator (up to 7 days) or freeze (up to 3 months). Discard any that show mold or off‑odors.

content.title: About
content.content: Nachos with chicken and beans is a popular Mexican‑style snack consisting of crunchy corn chips topped with grilled chicken, cooked beans, melted cheese and a blend of seasonings. It is often served with salsa, guacamole and sour cream.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Nachos originated in the United States in the 1940s as a quick bar snack in a Texas steak‑house.
The classic sauce for nachos is salsa verde, made from tomatillos, cilantro and lime.
Chicken used in nachos is typically grilled or baked, making it a leaner alternative to beef.
The beans are usually black or red, providing a good source of protein and fiber.
Nachos are often layered in a large platter so everyone can scoop their own portion.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Chicken and beans supply high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Contains dietary fiber
items.content: Beans add soluble and insoluble fiber that supports healthy digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Chicken and beans provide B6 and folate, important for metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: The dish provides iron, magnesium and potassium, which help maintain heart and muscle function.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Tomatoes, peppers and spices in the salsa are rich in lycopene and other antioxidants.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Cheese and prepared sauces can be salty, which may be problematic for hypertension.

items.title: Calorie dense
items.content: Corn chips and cheese make the dish energy‑rich; portion control is advised.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cheese can trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: Foodborne illness
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor salmonella; cook to an internal temperature of 75 °C.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the nachos hot, sprinkle with shredded cheese, add chicken, beans, salsa, guacamole and sour cream to taste. Fresh cilantro and a squeeze of lime brighten the flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in the refrigerator in an airtight container for up to 2 days. Keep chips separate from toppings to retain crunch.

content.title: About
content.content: Sopaipilla is a fried dough pastry traditional to South American countries, especially Chile and Argentina. It is served hot, often drizzled with sweet syrup or honey. The dough is made from flour, pumpkin or pumpkin puree, water, salt and yeast, then small pieces are deep‑fried until golden, giving a crisp exterior and a soft, slightly airy interior.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sopaipillas are a common street‑food snack and are also served in cafés as a quick dessert.
Traditional syrup is made from sugar, water and cinnamon, sometimes with orange zest.
Chile celebrates a "Sopaipilla Day" with regional contests for the most aromatic and crunchy version.
Pumpkin puree in the dough gives it a characteristic orange hue and a subtle flavor.
Sopaipillas are often used as a base for sweet burritos, filled with fruit, cream, or ice cream.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: The dough provides a quick source of energy from simple carbs, useful before physical activity.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: When whole‑grain flour or pumpkin is used, the pastry supplies dietary fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Yeast‑leavened dough contains small amounts of B1, B2 and niacin, important for metabolism.

items.title: Antioxidants in honey
items.content: Honey is rich in flavonoids and enzymes that may help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Minerals in syrup
items.content: Cinnamon‑spiced syrup provides trace calcium and iron.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Syrup and honey make the dish very sweet, which can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to tooth decay.

items.title: Honey allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to honey, especially those with pollen sensitivities.

items.title: Frying oil fat
items.content: Deep‑frying in large amounts of oil adds calories and may introduce trans fats if the oil is reused.

items.title: Undercooked interior
items.content: If the dough is not fried long enough, the inside can remain raw, increasing the risk of food‑borne illness.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve sopaipilla hot, drizzled with warm syrup or honey. It can be topped with fresh berries, whipped cream, ice cream, or a sprinkle of cinnamon. Eat it by hand as a street snack or cut into pieces for a plated dessert.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Sopaipilla is best enjoyed fresh and hot. If needed, keep it in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1‑2 days. For longer storage, cool and freeze; reheat in the oven before serving to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Tomato juice — a 100 % natural beverage made from ripe tomatoes without added sugar, preservatives or flavorings. It has a bright red color, characteristic aroma and a mildly sweet‑tart taste.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tomato juice is rich in lycopene, a powerful antioxidant that gives it the red hue.
Unlike ketchup, the juice contains no added sugar or salt.
Tomatoes for juice are often grown in greenhouses, allowing year‑round production.
Tomato juice is frequently used as a base for cocktails, soups and sauces.

items.title: High in vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C supports the immune system and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains lycopene
items.content: Lycopene has antioxidant properties and may help protect against cardiovascular disease.

items.title: Low calorie
items.content: Tomato juice is suitable for diet plans because it provides few calories per serving.

items.title: Source of potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate fluid balance and supports heart function.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: Tomato acids stimulate gastric juice production, improving digestion.

items.title: Tomato allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tomatoes or tomato juice.

items.title: High acidity
items.content: The acidity can irritate the stomach lining in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Some varieties may contain added salt; people with hypertension should check the label.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Tomato juice can be enjoyed chilled, used in smoothies, cocktails, soups, sauces and marinades. It is also added to vegetable stews to enhance flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the juice in the refrigerator after opening, in a tightly sealed container, for up to 5‑7 days. Unopened packages should be kept in a cool, dry place away from direct light.
